lessons.t: Decoding a word from its parts
lessons.intro: Many unfamiliar words are built from smaller pieces that each carry a fixed meaning. Learning those pieces lets you work out new words without reaching for a dictionary.

cards.b: Most long English words combine a root, which carries the core meaning, with optional prefixes before it and suffixes after it. Spotting these pieces gives you a way into the whole word.
The root holds the main idea, so look for it before anything else. Once you know it, the prefix and suffix show how that meaning is shifted or changed.
Test your working meaning in the sentence to make sure it fits. If it does not, reconsider where you split the word.

fig.title: Taking apart a word
fig.note: Combine the meaning of each part, then check it in the sentence.

ex.q: What does the word unbreakable most likely mean?
ex.why: The prefix un- means not and the suffix -able means able to be. Around the root break, they give not able to be broken, so option C is correct.

lessons.tip: Split the word, translate each piece, then join the meanings together.

quiz.q: In the word rewrite, what does the prefix re- mean?
quiz.why: The prefix re- means again, so rewrite means to write again.

quiz.q: Which suffix means full of?
quiz.why: The suffix -ful means full of, as in hopeful meaning full of hope.

lessons.t: Negative prefixes: un, in, non, dis
lessons.intro: Four prefixes turn many words into their opposites or their negatives. Spotting them quickly helps you read words like unsafe, incomplete and nonstop with confidence.

cards.b: Un-, in-, non- and dis- each add the sense of not or the opposite of to a root. Learn these four and you can decode a large number of everyday words.
In- becomes im- before b, m or p, il- before l, and ir- before r. So possible becomes impossible, legal becomes illegal and regular becomes irregular.
Dis- often means undo the action, as in connect and disconnect. When a word could be read two ways, check the sentence to see whether it means not or reverse.

fig.title: Pairs flipped by a prefix
fig.note: The root stays the same while the prefix reverses its meaning.

ex.q: Which word best means not safe?
ex.why: The prefix un- means not, so unsafe means not safe. Safeness is a noun for the quality of being safe, and resafe means to make safe again, so neither fits.

lessons.tip: Read the root first, then add the meaning of not to it.

quiz.q: What does the prefix non- mean in nonstop?
quiz.why: Non- means not, so nonstop means without stopping.

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of legal?
quiz.why: In- becomes il- before l, so the opposite of legal is illegal.

lessons.t: Number prefixes: uni, bi, tri, quad
lessons.intro: Number prefixes tell you how many of something there are, which helps with words about wheels, sides, cycles and parts. Knowing them lets you estimate a word's meaning from its opening letters.

cards.b: Uni means one, bi means two, tri means three and quad means four. They appear in words such as unicycle, bicycle, tricycle and quadrilateral.
Dec or deca means ten, as in decade, which is ten years. Centi means a hundredth, so a centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, and milli means a thousandth.
Multi means many, so a multitasker handles many tasks at once. Use the number prefix to estimate how many parts a thing has before you check its definition.

fig.title: Counting up from one
fig.note: Uni, bi, tri and quad count one to four. The next prefix, quin, means five.

ex.q: How many years is a decade?
ex.why: Dec means ten, so a decade is a span of ten years. A century is one hundred years, so the two words use different number roots.

lessons.tip: Learn number prefixes as a ladder: uni, bi, tri, quad, then penta for five.

quiz.q: What is a tricycle?
quiz.why: Tri means three, and cycle here means a wheeled vehicle, so a tricycle has three wheels.

quiz.q: What does centi mean in centimetre?
quiz.why: Centi means one hundredth, so a centimetre is one hundredth of a metre.

lessons.t: Time prefixes: pre, post, ante, retro
lessons.intro: Some prefixes place an event before or after another event in time. Recognising them helps you work out words such as prehistoric, postwar and retroactive without guessing.

cards.b: Pre- and ante- both mean before, as in preview and antedate. Post- means after, as in postwar, which describes the years following a war.

Prehistoric describes the time before written records existed, since pre- means before and historic relates to recorded history. Knowing the prefix turns an unfamiliar word into a clear picture of timing.
Retro- means backwards or back in time, so a retroactive pay rise applies to earlier months. You can see the same idea in retrospect, which means looking back on past events.

fig.title: Length of common time periods
fig.note: Decade, century and millennium name longer and longer spans of years.

ex.q: What does postwar describe?
ex.why: Post- means after, and war is the event, so postwar describes the period after a war. Prewar would be the opposite, describing the period before a war.

lessons.tip: Draw a quick timeline and place the event before, after or back in time.

quiz.q: What does antedate mean?
quiz.why: Ante- means before, so antedate means to date something earlier than it really is.

quiz.q: Which word describes a rule that applies to earlier events?
quiz.why: Retro means backwards, so a retroactive rule applies to past events.

lessons.t: Place prefixes: sub, super, inter, trans
lessons.intro: Prefixes of place describe where something sits or how something moves between or across things. They turn words like subsoil, superhuman and international into clear pictures.

cards.b: Sub- means under or below, as in subsoil, the layer beneath the topsoil. Super- means above, beyond or over, as in superhuman, which describes abilities beyond normal human limits.
Inter- means between or among, as in international, which involves several nations. Trans- means across or through, as in transatlantic, which crosses the Atlantic Ocean.
Picture the prefix as a direction before you read the root. A subway runs under the streets, so the sub- in subway matches its meaning of under.

fig.title: Two prefixes, two directions
fig.note: Sub- points down, while super- points up or beyond.

ex.q: Which word describes something that crosses the Atlantic Ocean?
ex.why: Trans- means across, so transatlantic describes something crossing the Atlantic. Sub- means under and super- means above, so those options describe position rather than crossing.

lessons.tip: Ask whether the prefix points under, over, between or across, then match it to the root.

quiz.q: What does subsoil describe?
quiz.why: Sub- means under, so subsoil is the layer beneath the topsoil.

quiz.q: What does superhuman mean?
quiz.why: Super- means above or beyond, so superhuman means beyond normal human ability.

lessons.t: The root port means carry
lessons.intro: The root port comes from Latin for carry, and it appears in many everyday words about moving things. Once you know it, words like export and portable become easy to decode.

cards.b: Port comes from the Latin portare, meaning to carry. Every word built on port keeps some sense of carrying, moving or bringing something from one place to another.
Ex- means out and im- means in, so export means to carry goods out of a country and import means to carry them in. Trans- means across, so transport moves people or goods across distances.
The suffix -able means able to be, so portable describes something that can be carried easily. A portfolio is a case for carrying papers, which keeps the same root idea.

fig.title: Goods moving between countries
fig.note: Port words show goods moving out, across and in.

ex.q: Which word means able to be carried around easily?
ex.why: Port means carry and -able means able to be, so portable means able to be carried around. The other options are about moving or bringing things, not describing something that can be carried.

lessons.tip: When you meet port, ask whether the prefix sends the carrying out, across or in.

quiz.q: What does transport mean at its root?
quiz.why: Trans means across and port means carry, so transport means to carry across.

quiz.q: What does import most likely mean?
quiz.why: In- becomes im- before p, so import means to carry something into a country.

lessons.t: The roots scrib and script mean write
lessons.intro: The root scrib, or its variant script, comes from Latin for write and appears in words about writing, describing and handwriting. Recognising it helps you decode both everyday and technical words.

cards.b: Scrib and script both come from the Latin scribere, meaning to write. A scribe copied documents by hand, and a script is any written text, such as a film script.
De- means down, so describe means to write down in words. Pre- means before, so prescribe means to set out a rule or treatment in advance.
Manuscript combines manu, meaning hand, with script, so it is a document written by hand. Inscription combines in with script, so it is writing cut or written into a surface.

fig.title: Decoding a scrib word
fig.note: Describe: de- (down) plus scrib (write) gives write down.

ex.q: What does prescribe mean?
o: To set a rule in advance
ex.why: Pre- means before and scrib means write, so prescribe means to set out a rule or treatment in advance. The other options misread the prefix or confuse the root with copying or listing.

lessons.tip: Scrib and script both mean write, so whenever you see either, think of writing first.

quiz.q: What is a manuscript?
quiz.why: Manu means hand, so a manuscript is a document written by hand.

quiz.q: What does describe mean in its parts?
quiz.why: De- means down and scrib means write, so describe means to write down in words.

lessons.t: The root dict means say or speak
lessons.intro: The root dict comes from Latin for say or speak and appears in words about speaking, telling and judging. Learning it helps you decode words like predict, dictate and contradict.

cards.b: The root dict comes from the Latin dicere, meaning to say or speak. A dictionary lists words and their meanings, and to dictate means to say words aloud for someone else to write down.
Pre- means before, so predict means to say what will happen beforehand. Contra- means against, so contradict means to say the opposite of what someone has said.
Verdict combines ver, meaning true, with dict, so it is a true saying given as a decision. Judges and juries deliver verdicts at the end of a trial.

fig.title: Roots learned in this module
fig.note: Learn each root as one short meaning, then build words from it.

ex.q: What does predict mean?
ex.why: Pre- means before and dict means say, so predict means to say what will happen beforehand. The other options place the prefix in the wrong position in time or change the meaning of the root.

lessons.tip: Say the prefix meaning and the root meaning out loud, then join them together.

quiz.q: What does dictate mean?
o: To say aloud for someone to write
quiz.why: Dictate uses dict, meaning say, so dictate means to say words aloud for someone else to record.

quiz.q: What does contradict mean?
o: To say the same thing again
To speak against what was said
quiz.why: Contra means against, so contradict means to say the opposite of what someone has said.

lessons.t: How analogy questions work
lessons.intro: Analogy questions give you a pair of words and ask you to find a second pair with the same relationship. Naming the link first makes these questions quick to solve.

cards.b: Turn the first pair into a short sentence, such as a wheel is part of a car. The link you name becomes the test for the matching pair.
Common links include part to whole, tool to purpose, cause to effect and opposites. Choose the most precise link, because loose links let several options look right.
Apply the same sentence pattern to each answer and reject any pair that breaks it. The right answer should fit exactly, not roughly.

fig.title: Solving an analogy in four moves
fig.note: Name the link before you look at the answer options.

ex.q: Pen is to write as knife is to what?
ex.why: A pen is a tool used for writing, so the link is tool to purpose. A knife is a tool used for cutting, so cut is the matching purpose.

lessons.tip: Say the link as a short sentence before you read any answer options.

quiz.q: Wheel is to car as page is to what?
quiz.why: A wheel is a part of a car, so a page is a part of a book.

quiz.q: Hunger is to eating as thirst is to what?
quiz.why: Hunger is the feeling that prompts eating, so thirst is the feeling that prompts drinking.

lessons.t: Part to whole relationships
lessons.intro: Many analogies compare a part with the whole it belongs to, such as a wheel and a car. Spotting this link helps you solve questions that ask for a missing part or a missing whole.

cards.b: A part is a component that sits inside a larger whole, such as a finger on a hand. The whole is the object that contains and completes its parts.
Some pairs have a set count, such as twelve months in a year or six faces on a cube. Counting the parts can confirm that a pair is a true part-whole link.
A page is part of a book, so the link runs from the part to the whole. The reverse pairing, book to page, does not describe the same relationship.

fig.title: Parts within a whole
fig.note: A half dozen is a part of a dozen, so six is part of twelve.

ex.q: Scene is to play as chapter is to what?
ex.why: A scene is a section that makes up part of a play, so a chapter is a section that makes up part of a book. The other options relate to theatre or performance rather than the whole that chapters make up.

lessons.tip: A part-whole pair usually reads as one of the pieces that make up the whole.

quiz.q: Spoke is to wheel as finger is to what?
quiz.why: A spoke is one part of a wheel, so a finger is one part of a hand.

quiz.q: Brick is to wall as tree is to what?
quiz.why: A brick is one part of a wall, so a tree is one part of a forest.

lessons.t: Cause and effect pairs
lessons.intro: Some analogies pair a cause with the effect it produces, such as heat and melting. Identifying the direction, from cause to result, helps you choose the right partner.

cards.b: A cause is the event that makes something happen, and the effect is what follows as a result. Rain causes puddles, so a puddle is an effect of rain.
Cause to effect runs in one direction, so the reverse pairing usually fails. A puddle does not cause rain in the usual sense, so puddle to rain is a weak match.
Phrases such as leads to, produces or results in help you name the link. Try the phrase in a sentence to confirm the cause comes first.

fig.title: Cause and effect side by side
fig.note: The cause comes first, and the effect follows as its result.

ex.q: Heat is to melting as cold is to what?
ex.why: Heat causes melting, so cold causes freezing, which is its effect on liquids such as water. Winter is a season linked to cold, not the result that cold produces.

lessons.tip: Ask what happens because of this to find the effect in any pair.

quiz.q: Study is to knowledge as exercise is to what?
quiz.why: Studying produces knowledge, just as exercise produces fitness.

quiz.q: Which pair shows cause and effect?
quiz.why: Rain causes the ground to become wet, so rain comes first and wet ground follows.

lessons.t: Matching a tool to its purpose
lessons.intro: Many analogies link a tool with the purpose it serves, such as a spoon and eating. Knowing this link lets you answer questions about what a tool is used for and who uses it.

cards.b: A tool is an object made to perform a specific task, so its purpose defines it. A ladder exists to reach high places, so reaching is its function.
Some analogies ask who uses the tool, like a surgeon with a scalpel. Decide whether the question asks about the object, the user or the result.
A thermometer measures temperature and a ruler measures length. This pattern appears often, so name the quantity each instrument measures.

fig.title: From need to tool to result
fig.note: Pick the tool that matches the task, then check the result.

ex.q: Thermometer is to temperature as ruler is to what?
ex.why: A thermometer is the instrument that measures temperature, so a ruler is the instrument that measures length. Weight is measured by a scale, not a ruler.

lessons.tip: Name the quantity a tool measures or creates, then match it to the second word.

quiz.q: Scalpel is to surgeon as brush is to what?
quiz.why: A scalpel is a tool used by a surgeon, and a brush is a tool used by a painter.

quiz.q: Clock is to time as scale is to what?
quiz.why: A clock measures time and a scale measures weight.

lessons.t: Degrees of intensity
lessons.intro: Some analogies compare words that differ only in strength, such as warm and hot. Spotting the scale of intensity helps you match a pair that shows the same size of difference.

cards.b: Degree pairs share a core meaning but differ in how strong it is. Warm and hot both describe heat, but hot is the more intense of the two.
Read the pair in order, so warm to hot and damp to soaked both rise. Keep the same direction when you test the options.
Some words sit close together on the scale, while others are far apart. The correct answer matches both the direction and the size of the step.

fig.title: Rising intensity of wetness
fig.note: Each word is a stronger degree of the same quality.

ex.q: Warm is to hot as cool is to what?
ex.why: Warm is a milder form of hot, and cool is a milder form of cold. Both pairs rise in the same degree of intensity, from weaker to stronger.

lessons.tip: Put the two words on a scale before you judge whether the pattern matches.

quiz.q: Annoyed is to furious as tired is to what?
quiz.why: Both pairs move from a mild feeling to a far stronger one, so exhausted is the stronger form of tired.

quiz.q: Which word expresses the strongest feeling?
quiz.why: Delighted expresses a much stronger happiness than the other three words.

lessons.t: Opposites and antonym pairs
lessons.intro: Antonym analogies pair words with their opposites, such as hot and cold. Recognising that the two words sit at opposite ends of one scale helps you choose the matching pair quickly.

cards.b: Antonyms sit at opposite ends of the same quality, like hot and cold on a temperature scale. Each pair is defined by one shared dimension.
A word close in meaning, such as timid for cowardly, is a synonym rather than an opposite. Analogy options often include these to trap you.
Good opposites match in strength, so a strong word pairs with another strong word. Stingy is the right partner for generous, because thrifty is a milder and more positive word.

fig.title: Common opposite pairs
fig.note: Opposites sit at either end of one shared scale.

ex.q: Brave is to cowardly as generous is to what?
ex.why: Brave and cowardly are opposites at either end of one scale of courage. Generous and stingy form the same kind of strong opposite pair, while kind, wealthy and thrifty are not its opposite.

lessons.tip: A good antonym often describes the same trait from the other end.

quiz.q: Which word is the antonym of ancient?
quiz.why: Modern is the opposite of ancient, at the far end of the age scale.

quiz.q: Which pair is opposites?
quiz.why: Shallow and deep sit at opposite ends of the depth scale, while the other pairs are close synonyms.

lessons.t: Linking a worker to a workplace
lessons.intro: Some analogies connect a person with the place where they usually do their work. Recognising the typical setting for a job helps you solve these questions by linking role and place.

cards.b: Many jobs are tied to a typical place, such as a chef in a kitchen or a pilot in a cockpit. These pairs test whether you know the everyday setting for a role.
Ask what the worker does and where that activity happens, since a teacher teaches in a classroom. The place is usually where the main task takes place.
Options may include a place linked to a different job, such as a stage, which suits an actor but not a chef. Check that the place fits the main task, not just the subject area.

fig.title: Pairing a job with its setting
fig.note: Ask where this worker usually does the main task.

ex.q: Pilot is to cockpit as teacher is to what?
ex.why: A pilot works in a cockpit, and a teacher works in a classroom. An airport is where pilots go, but it is not the specific place where the pilot does the work.

lessons.tip: Name the activity first, then the room where that activity happens.

quiz.q: Surgeon is to operating theatre as chef is to what?
quiz.why: A surgeon usually works in an operating theatre, and a chef usually works in a kitchen.

quiz.q: Librarian is to library as farmer is to what?
quiz.why: A librarian works in a library, and a farmer does most of their work in a field.

lessons.t: Solving a two-step analogy
lessons.intro: A two-step analogy chains two relationships, so the middle word belongs to both pairs. Your answer must respect both links, not just the first one you notice.

cards.b: A two-step analogy chains two relationships together, and the middle word links them. The answer must follow both links, not just the first one you spot.
The bridge word connects the two steps. In page, book, library, the word book is the bridge.
Read the full chain out loud from the first word to the answer. If each step reads naturally, you have found the right answer.

fig.title: Working through two links
fig.note: Name each link, then confirm the answer matches both.

ex.q: Page is to book as book is to what?
ex.why: A page is a part that makes up a book, and a book is an item kept inside a library. The second pair therefore moves from one item to the larger place where it is stored.

lessons.tip: Look for the word that appears in both pairs, since it is the bridge.

quiz.q: Seed is to plant as egg is to what?
quiz.why: A seed grows into a plant, and an egg hatches into a chick.

quiz.q: Cup is to tea as bowl is to what?
quiz.why: A cup is a container used for holding tea, and a bowl is a container used for holding soup.

lessons.t: Why exact words beat vague ones
lessons.intro: Exact words carry a precise meaning, so readers picture what you picture. Vague words leave readers guessing, which weakens both writing and speech.

cards.b: Words such as thing, good and nice can fit almost anything, so they tell the reader very little. Replacing them with precise words sharpens the message at once.
Walked, strolled, marched and trudged all describe movement, but each shows a different pace and mood. Pick the one that matches what actually happened.
Ask whether a reader could picture only one thing from your word. If several images are possible, search for a more exact choice.

fig.title: Vague versus exact
fig.note: Exact words narrow the picture to what you actually mean.

ex.q: Which verb best describes walking slowly and with difficulty?
ex.why: Trudged describes walking slowly and heavily, often from tiredness. Went, moved and got are vague because they could describe almost any movement.

lessons.tip: Replace each vague word with the one detail it stands for.

quiz.q: Which sentence is the most exact?
o: The day was warm and sunny.
quiz.why: Warm and sunny name the exact qualities of the day, whereas nice, fine and good are vague.

quiz.q: Which word is more exact than said for speaking in a very quiet voice?
quiz.why: Whispered shows the quiet manner of speech, while spoke, told and mentioned say little about how it was said.

lessons.t: Connotation: the feeling behind a word
lessons.intro: Two words can share a meaning yet carry different feelings, and that emotional charge is called connotation. Choosing the connotation that fits your purpose keeps your tone accurate.

cards.b: Denotation is the literal meaning of a word, as listed in a dictionary. Slim, skinny and thin all denote a small body size, so they share a basic meaning.
Slim usually sounds approving, skinny often sounds negative, and scrawny suggests weakness. The same body size reads differently depending on the word you choose.
Use a positive connotation when praising, and a neutral one when reporting facts. Ask what feeling you want the reader to take from the sentence.

fig.title: Reading a word's emotional charge
fig.note: Pick the word whose feeling suits the moment.

ex.q: Which word has the most positive connotation for someone who spends carefully?
ex.why: Thrifty describes careful spending in an approving way. Stingy, cheap and mean all carry a negative judgement.

lessons.tip: Read the sentence aloud and listen for whether the word sounds like praise or criticism.

quiz.q: Which word carries a negative connotation?
quiz.why: Pushy suggests someone is too forceful, while the other three words sound positive.

quiz.q: Which word is the most neutral for a factual report?
quiz.why: Reportedly simply says that something was reported, without praise or criticism.

lessons.t: Specific nouns beat general ones
lessons.intro: Specific nouns name one particular thing, while general nouns cover a whole group. Choosing specific nouns makes your writing clearer and more vivid.

cards.b: Words such as vehicle, animal and food cover a wide range of things. They suit a broad overview but leave the reader unsure which one you mean.
Hatchback, beagle and risotto name one particular kind of vehicle, animal or food. They give the reader a clear and memorable image.
Start with the general noun, then ask what kind you mean until you reach a precise one. Stop when the reader can picture exactly what you intend.

fig.title: From general to specific
fig.note: Each step narrows the group, so the last word is most precise.

ex.q: Which noun is the most specific?
ex.why: Creature, animal and bird are broad groups, with creature being the widest. Robin names one particular species, so it is the most specific.

lessons.tip: When a noun feels safe, ask what kind of it you mean and replace it.

quiz.q: Which phrase is the most specific?
quiz.why: Cathedral names one specific type of building, while the other options describe broad categories.

quiz.q: Which is the most precise word for a kind of fruit?
quiz.why: Strawberry names one specific fruit, whereas food, snack and berry are broader categories.

lessons.t: Strong verbs carry more meaning
lessons.intro: Strong verbs show exactly how an action happens, so you often need no extra adverbs. Weak verbs leave the detail to adverbs, which can make writing feel flat.

cards.b: Verbs such as go, get, make and put are useful but general, so they often need an adverb or phrase for detail. This can make a sentence wordy and flat.
Stroll, sprint and grab each hold a specific manner inside the verb itself. A single strong verb is usually shorter and more vivid than a weak one plus an adverb.
When a verb is followed by an adverb, ask whether one stronger verb could replace both. For example, walked quickly can become hurried, dashed or sprinted.

fig.title: General verb and exact choices
fig.note: Each row starts with a general verb, then gives exact choices.

ex.q: Which single verb best replaces walked very quickly?
ex.why: Hurried means walked in a rushed way, so it packs the speed into one word. Strolled means the opposite, while moved and went are too general to show the speed.

lessons.tip: When an adverb hangs on a weak verb, look for one verb that holds both ideas.

quiz.q: Which verb is strongest in: The cat ___ across the garden?
quiz.why: Dashed captures speed and movement in one word, while went, got and did are weak.

quiz.q: Which verb best replaces said loudly?
quiz.why: Shouted carries the loud manner inside the verb, so no adverb is needed.

lessons.t: Affect or effect: choosing the right word
lessons.intro: Affect and effect look alike and are easily confused, but they usually play different grammatical roles. Knowing the usual role helps you choose correctly in most sentences.

cards.b: Affect means to influence or change something, as in the weather will affect our plans. In everyday writing it is almost always a verb.
Effect means a result, as in the effect of the storm was severe. A useful memory aid is that effect is the outcome, and an outcome is a noun.
Effect can be a verb meaning to bring about, as in to effect change. Affect is a noun only in specialist psychology writing, so you rarely need it.

fig.title: Choosing affect or effect
fig.note: Ask whether the word is an action or a result.

ex.q: Choose the correct word: The new rule will ___ how we work.
ex.why: Here the word is a verb meaning to influence, so affect fits. Effect would be a noun, which does not fit the space, and effective and affection are different words.

lessons.tip: Swap in the word influence, and if it fits, use affect.

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: The medicine had a strong ___ on his recovery.
quiz.why: Effect is a noun here meaning result, and a strong effect on recovery is a result.

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: Heavy rain will ___ the match.
quiz.why: Affect is a verb meaning to influence, so will affect the match means will influence it.

lessons.t: Hedging words: certain, likely, possible
lessons.intro: Hedging words show how sure you are, so readers know how far to rely on a claim. Picking the right level prevents you from overstating or understating what you know.

cards.b: Words such as certainly, likely, possibly and unlikely tell the reader how confident you are in a statement. They are precise tools, not filler.
Use certainly only when the evidence is conclusive, such as two plus two making four. Use possibly when there is some chance but little proof.
Saying something will definitely happen when you only suspect it can mislead readers. Piling on maybes can make you sound unsure, so aim for the level your evidence supports.

fig.title: Rough certainty of each word
fig.note: Percentages are rough guides to how sure each word sounds.

ex.q: A forecast gives a 75 per cent chance of rain. Which word best describes this?
ex.why: A 75 per cent chance is well above even odds, so likely fits best. Possibly suggests much lower confidence, while certainly would need a 100 per cent chance.

lessons.tip: Match your hedge to a rough percentage in your head before you write it.

quiz.q: Which sentence states a small chance with the right confidence?
o: It is possible that it fails.
quiz.why: A small chance calls for possible, while certainly and definitely overstate the claim and the past tense states it as fact.

quiz.q: Which word matches very probable but not guaranteed?
quiz.why: Likely means probable and strongly expected, while certainly claims total certainty.

lessons.t: Borrow or lend: same act, two sides
lessons.intro: Some pairs of words describe the same event from opposite sides, such as borrow and lend. Choosing the right one depends on who is giving and who is receiving.

cards.b: Borrow and lend both describe an item passing from one person to another for a while. The difference lies in which person the sentence is describing.
To borrow is to take something from someone with the intention of returning it. The receiver asks, may I borrow your pen?
To lend is to give something to someone for a time, expecting it back. The giver is asked, can you lend me your pen?

fig.title: Borrow and lend compared
fig.note: The same loan is described from two different sides.

ex.q: Maria asks her brother, Can you ___ me ten pounds until Friday?
ex.why: Lend fits because her brother is the one giving the money, so the request is for him to lend it. Borrow would describe Maria receiving it, which does not fit a request made to her brother.

lessons.tip: Ask whether the subject is giving or receiving, then choose lend or borrow.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses lend correctly?
o: I will lend the book from you.
Could you lend me a pen?
I lent a pen from you.
She lent me her coat for borrowing.
quiz.why: Lend takes the giver as subject and the receiver as object, so could you lend me a pen is correct.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses borrow correctly?
o: Can you borrow me your umbrella?
quiz.why: Borrow means taking something temporarily, so the speaker is the one receiving the umbrella.

lessons.t: Replacing vague words like thing
lessons.intro: Vague words such as thing, stuff and get appear constantly in everyday writing but hide your real meaning. Spotting and replacing them is one of the quickest ways to improve clarity.

cards.b: Thing, stuff, get and do can stand in for almost any noun or verb. When you see them, the reader has to guess what you meant.
Imagine someone asking, what exactly is that thing? Your answer is the precise word to use, such as the report or the spreadsheet.
Sometimes a vague phrase can be deleted without losing meaning, as with the fact that. Remove filler first, then name anything still unclear.

fig.title: Turning vague words into exact ones
fig.note: Repeat the loop for every vague word in the draft.

ex.q: Which revision is most precise? Original: We need to get some things for the event.
o: We need to get stuff for the event.
We need to buy plates and chairs for the event.
We need some things for the event.
We need to do the things for the event.
ex.why: Buy names the action, and plates and chairs name the items, so the reader knows exactly what is needed. The other options keep vague words such as get, stuff, things or do.

lessons.tip: If you cannot name the thing, you probably do not yet know what you are trying to say.

quiz.q: Which sentence is most exact?
quiz.why: Report names the specific item, whereas thing, stuff and it leave the reader guessing.

quiz.q: Which version removes filler without losing meaning?
o: The fact that the team won was exciting.
The team was won, which was exciting.
quiz.why: Dropping the fact that gives a tighter sentence while keeping the same meaning.
